items.title: Stratified Modeling for Imbalanced Data
items.author: Jason Bryer
items.description:
NOTE: Any updates to this article will be maintained here: https://medley.bryer.org/articles/stratified_glm.html
Introduction



Continue reading: Stratified Modeling for Imbalanced Data
items.content:
[This article was first published on Jason Bryer, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

NOTE: Any updates to this article will be maintained here: https://medley.bryer.org/articles/stratified_glm.html

Introduction

Statistical modeling when there is substantial imbalance in the dependent variable poses unique challenges. In these situations models often favor the majority class. Two common approaches are upsampling and downsampling. Upsampling is the process of increasing the sampling of the minority group to more closely match the size of the majority group. Conversely, downsampling involves sampling from the majority group to more closely match the size of the minority group. The latter is generally not preferred since it artificially increases the sample size (i.e. n) resulting in decreasing the standard error estimates.1 This paper introduces an approach where multiple logistic regression models are estimated using the minority group and a unique subset of the majority group such that all observations are majority observations are used in exactly one model while the minority group is reused across models. The final model pools the models using Rubin’s Rules defined within the context of multiple imputation (Rubin, 2004).

Impact on Fitted Values

In the United States there are broadly two types of schools, public and private. Public schools are funded by property taxes whereas privates schools charge tuition to the families. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is an international evaluation managed by the OECD. It measures how well 15-year-old students apply their knowledge and problem-solving skills in reading, mathematics, and science to real-world challenges. PISA samples students from both public and private schools within the United States. The medley package contains a subset of the PISA data for the United States containing 5233 observations of 44 variables. There are 4888 public school students and 345 private school students (6.5927766%)

To exemplify the problem with estimating logistic regression with imbalanced data, let’s consider several models where the ratio of public-to-private schools varies from 1-to-1 to 14-to-1. Figure @ref(fig:shrinking-values) represents the distributions of the fitted values from a logistic regression with varying ratios of public-to-private schools. That is, all private school students were used in every model. For the 1-to-1 model, the first 345 public school observations, then for the 2-to-1 model the first 690 observations, etcetera until the final model uses all observations. The vertical lines correspond to the median fitted values. With all else equal, as the ratio of public-to-private schools increases, the range of fitted values shrinks towards the majority group.2

Stratified Modeling

The goal of stratified modeling is to address imbalance in the outcome variable while still leveraging all data. The first step is to separate the majority and minority classes. Observations in the minority class will be used in all model estimations. Observations in the majority class will be randomly assigned a model. The number of models is determined by the extent of the imbalance the specified ratio of majority-to-minority observations (the default is 1). For the PISA data here, there are approximately 14 times as many public school observations to private school observations. Using a ratio of one we will estimate 14 models. It should be noted that the public schools students will be used in exactly one model whereas the private school students will be used in all models. The stratified_glm() performs the modeling. To maximize flexibility this function can pass any parameter to the stats::glm() function. However, parameters that reference specific observations (e.g. weights, subset) should not be used since stats::glm() will be called with subsets of the data that will not match the order of the data. Similarly, the family parameter defaults to binomial(link='logit') since this method only works with classification problems with two classes.

results <- medley::stratified_glm(
    formula = Private ~ .,
    data = pisa,
    ratio = 1
)

The results of all the models are combined using the mitools::MIcombine function (Lumley, 2026). Although this approach is designed for combining multiple imputed data sets, in this case it allows us to have a single coefficient and standard error that is not artificially smaller given a larger sample size for a model. The fitted values from all the individual models is available in the fitted element of the returned object. Additionally, the individual model results are available in the model element. The summary() function returns a data frame with the combined coefficients, standard error, and p-value. Below only coefficients where p < 0.1 is printed to save space.

pisa_summary <- summary(results)
pisa_summary |> dplyr::filter(p < 0.1)
                     coefficients   se     p
(Intercept)                 -5.21 2.63 0.051
ST04Q01Male                  0.84 0.28 0.004
ST08Q04TRUE                 -0.50 0.27 0.071
ST08Q05TRUE                  0.75 0.36 0.038
ST20Q06TRUE                  1.79 0.95 0.060
ST20Q07TRUE                  0.72 0.31 0.021
ST21Q05Three or more         0.93 0.45 0.042
ST22Q01201-500 books         1.18 0.59 0.050

Figure @ref(fig:fitted-distributions) plots the density distributions from the full model (single model using all data) and the stratified models. The stratified sample shows a distribution that spans the entire range of fitted values resulting in fitted values that are more interpretable.

plot(results)

Predictions for new data can be estimated using the predict() function.

pisa_predicted <- predict(results, newdata = pisa)
head(pisa_predicted)
   1    2    3    4    5    6 
0.79 0.16 0.30 0.24 0.22 0.46

Figure @ref(fig:fitted-distributions-3) shows how the stratified modeling is less effective when the ratio of public-to-private students increases to 3-to-1.

medley::stratified_glm(
    formula = Private ~ .,
    data = pisa,
    ratio = 3
) |> plot()

Impact for Predictive Modeling

Stratified modeling clearly provides a strategy for addressing the issue of shrinking fitted values from logistic regression as imbalance in the outcome increases. In this section we will explore what impact, if any, does this approach have when modeling for prediction. To begin, we will split our data into a training and validation data set with 80% for training and 20% for validation.

set.seed(2112); split <- medley::stratified_split(pisa, 'Private', 0.8)
pisa_train <- split$train
pisa_valid <- split$validation
pisa_train$Private |> table() |> prop.table()
FALSE  TRUE 
0.934 0.066 
pisa_valid$Private |> table() |> prop.table()
FALSE  TRUE 
0.934 0.066

Full Model

First, we will estimate the logistic regression model using the full data set.

full_model <- glm(Private ~ ., data = pisa_train, family = binomial(link = 'logit'))

Get the predictions for the validation data set.

full_new_predictions <- predict(full_model, newdata = pisa_valid, type = 'response')

We calculate the metrics for a receiver operating characteristic below. The summary function provides us with some thresholds that maximize accuracy, minimize cost3, or where the specificity and sensitivity curves intersect.

full_roc <- medley::calculate_roc(
    predictions = full_new_predictions,
    observed = pisa_valid$Private
)
summary(full_roc)
AUC = 0.747
Cost of false-positive = 1
Cost of false-negative = 1
Threshold with minimum cost = 0.465 (accuracy = 93.4%)
Threshold with maximum accuracy = 0.465 (accuracy = 93.4%)
Sensitivity and specificity intersection = 0.059 (accuracy = 66.4%)

Figure @ref(fig:full-roc) represents the receiver operating characteristic plot for the validation data using the full model.

plot(full_roc)

In order to balance sensitivity and specificity we provide a confusion matrix using the intersection of these two curves as the cut point for determing the outcome class.

medley::confusion_matrix(
    observed = pisa_valid$Private,
    predicted = full_new_predictions > attr(full_roc, 'intersection')
)
              predicted             
  observed        FALSE         TRUE
     FALSE 649 (61.99%) 329 (31.42%)
      TRUE   23 (2.20%)   46 (4.39%)
Accuracy: 66.38%
Sensitivity: 66.36%
Specificity: 66.67%

Stratified Model

Now let’s estimate the stratified model.

stratified_model <- medley::stratified_glm(
    formula = Private ~ .,
    data = pisa_train,
    ratio = 1
)
stratified_new_predictions <- predict(stratified_model, newdata = pisa_valid)

Examine the receiver operating characteristics to determine the optimal cut point. Figure @ref(fig:stratified-roc) plots the results.

stratified_roc <- medley::calculate_roc(
    predictions = stratified_new_predictions,
    observed = pisa_valid$Private
)
summary(stratified_roc)
AUC = 0.745
Cost of false-positive = 1
Cost of false-negative = 1
Threshold with minimum cost = 1 (accuracy = 93.4%)
Threshold with maximum accuracy = 1 (accuracy = 93.4%)
Sensitivity and specificity intersection = 0.509 (accuracy = 68.6%)
plot(stratified_roc)

Finally, calculate the confusion matrix using the intersection of the sensitivity and specificity curves as the cut point for determing predicted class.

medley::confusion_matrix(
    observed = pisa_valid$Private,
    predicted = full_new_predictions > attr(stratified_roc, 'intersection')
)
              predicted          
  observed        FALSE      TRUE
     FALSE 975 (93.12%) 3 (0.29%)
      TRUE   68 (6.49%) 1 (0.10%)
Accuracy: 93.22%
Sensitivity: 99.69%
Specificity: 1.45%

Often introductory texts for predictive modeling and logistic regression suggest using a cut point of 0.5 for determining the class. As show above, this is not the optimal cut point when there is significant imbalance. The stratified modeling approach introduced gets us closer to that intuitive cut point in the middle. It should be noted that this approach is no better or worse for making predictions. However, it does address the issue of shrinking fitted values and makes the fitted and predicted values more interpretable.

Conclusion

The stratified modeling approach provides a modeling approach for logistic regression where interpretability of the fitted or predicted values are meaningful. For predictive modeling adjusting the cut point for making a class prediction will provide a similar result. However, this issue was initially encountered when conducting propensity score analysis (PSA). Logistic regression is often used to estimate the propensity scores, which are defined as the conditional probability of being in the treatment (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). When using logistic regression, the propensity scores are simply the fitted values from the model. In this context having fitted values that span the entire range where the distribution of the treatment group (private schools in this example) is skewed to the right and the control group (public schools in this example) is skewed to the left. For these situations the stratified modeling approach may provide a reasonable approach to addressing the issue of shrinking fitted values from logistic regression with significant imbalance.

References

Bryer, Jason M., “A national study comparing charter and traditional public schools using propensity score analysis” (2014). Legacy Theses & Dissertations (2009 - 2024). 1090. https://doi.org/10.54014/H2BR-2XKN

Lumley, T (2026). mitools: Tools for Multiple Imputation of Missing Data_. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.mitools. R package version 2.7, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=mitools.

Rosenbaum, P.R., & Rubin, D.B. (1983). The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika, 70(1), 41–55, https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/70.1.41

Rubin DB. Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys. New York: John Wiley and Sons; 2004.

Footnotes

  1. The for all fixed .︎

  2. See https://psa.bryer.org/appendix-psranges.html for a simulation showing the same result.︎

  3. Since the costs of false-positives and false-negatives are the same this will be the same threshold as maximizing accuracy︎

items.title: Introducing tuiksdmx: A Metadata-Driven R Client for Turkish Official Statistics
items.author: M. Fatih Tüzen
items.description:
The tuiksdmx R package logo
1 Introduction



Continue reading: Introducing tuiksdmx: A Metadata-Driven R Client for Turkish Official Statistics
items.content:
[This article was first published on A Statistician's R Notebook, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

1 Introduction

Accessing official statistics programmatically should be straightforward. In practice, however, finding the right dataset is only part of the problem. An analyst also needs to understand its dimensions, available classifications, valid codes, and the structure of the request accepted by the data provider.

This is particularly relevant for SDMX (Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange), the international standard widely used to exchange statistical data and metadata. SDMX provides a consistent framework for describing multidimensional statistical datasets, but it does not eliminate the need to understand their structures.

I developed tuiksdmx, an open-source R package that provides an authenticated, metadata-driven interface to the Turkish Statistical Institute’s (TÜİK, or TurkStat) SDMX REST service. The goal is not simply to download data. It is to make the steps leading to a valid and reproducible request easier to discover, understand, and verify.

The project is available on GitHub, with detailed guides and function documentation on its dedicated website.

2 Why a Metadata-Driven Client?

An SDMX dataset is not necessarily a conventional rectangular table waiting to be downloaded. A particular Dataflow is associated with a Data Structure Definition (DSD), which specifies the dimensions used to identify a statistical series. These dimensions may reference Codelists defining permitted values, while Concepts describe what the dimensions represent.

A typical workflow therefore involves several questions:

  1. Which Dataflow contains the statistics I need?
  2. What dimensions and classifications define that Dataflow?
  3. Which codes are valid for the relevant dimensions?
  4. How can I request observations without assembling a raw SDMX key by hand?

tuiksdmx brings these steps together. It supports Dataflow discovery, DSD and Codelist inspection, metadata-based filter validation, structure-aware key construction, and observation retrieval. It also helps distinguish between the codes defined in metadata and those actually present in returned data.

The distinction matters: a code being valid does not mean that observations exist for it in every period.

3 Getting Started

3.1 Install the package

Version 0.1.0 is distributed through GitHub; it is not currently on CRAN. Install it with pak:

install.packages("pak")  # If needed
pak::pak("MFatihTuzen/tuiksdmx")

library(tuiksdmx)

3.2 Configure authentication

The TÜİK SDMX service currently requires authentication for its data endpoints. tuiksdmx accepts an API key and handles the authentication workflow internally. For regular use, I recommend storing the key in your personal .Renviron file, rather than embedding credentials in an R script.

TUIK_SDMX_API_KEY=YOUR_OWN_API_KEY

You can open that file using usethis::edit_r_environ() if you have usethis installed. Restart R after saving it. The package will then read the environment variable automatically.

Never publish your API key or access tokens in a script, blog post, repository, or issue report. You must obtain and configure your own credentials; installing the package does not provide an API key.

3.3 Find a Dataflow

Instead of starting with a hard-coded endpoint, search the available Dataflows by subject:

# Search by an English description
flows <- tuik_search_dataflows(
  "consumer price",
  language = "en",
  limit = 10
)

flows

You can also search in Turkish, for example with tuik_search_dataflows("tüketici fiyat"). This makes discovery possible without knowing the Dataflow identifier in advance.

3.4 Explore dimensions before retrieving data

The following example uses the consumer price Dataflow DF_TUFE_SDMX_TT01, inspected during package development. Since provider catalogues can evolve, always check the current metadata before building a production workflow.

# Explore the structure without retrieving observations
tuik_explore("DF_TUFE_SDMX_TT01")

# Inspect the codes associated with one dimension
tuik_explore(
  "DF_TUFE_SDMX_TT01",
  dimension = "DEGISIM"
)

This is one of the central design decisions behind the package: understand the data structure first, then request observations. It reduces the need to guess dimension identifiers or construct query keys manually.

3.5 Retrieve observations

Once the relevant Dataflow and period are known, retrieving data can be concise:

cpi <- tuik_get_data(
  "DF_TUFE_SDMX_TT01",
  start_period = "2026-01",
  end_period   = "2026-01"
)

head(cpi)

There is an important qualification: this request retrieves all series for the selected observation period, not just one CPI indicator. Restricting the time range alone does not guarantee a small response.

For a more focused query, the package accepts named, metadata-validated dimension filters:

selected <- list(
  REF_AREA = "TR",
  FREQ = "M",
  DEGISIM = "1",
  SINIFLAMA_DUZEYI = "2"
)

# Validate the chosen values against the Dataflow structure
tuik_explore(
  "DF_TUFE_SDMX_TT01",
  filters = selected
)

A practical limitation is worth highlighting. Complete series-key filters allow the package to construct a targeted server-side SDMX request. Partial filters, on the other hand, require an explicit allow_all = TRUE opt-in and may lead to a broader download followed by filtering in R. The package does not present this as an efficient server-side partial-key request, nor does allow_all impose a data-size limit. The filtering and performance guide explains the distinction in detail.

4 A Subtle but Important Question: Which Codes Actually Have Data?

Metadata and observed data answer different questions.

A Codelist defines the theoretical set of codes for a dimension. But some of those codes may not appear in the observations returned for a particular period and set of filters.

tuiksdmx addresses this distinction through two complementary operations:

profile <- tuik_flow_profile("DF_TUFE_SDMX_TT01")

# Permitted codes in the metadata
tuik_dimension_codes(profile, dimension = "DEGISIM")

# Codes observed in the data for a bounded request
observed <- tuik_available_codes(
  profile,
  dimension = "COICOP_2018",
  start_period = "2026-01",
  end_period = "2026-01",
  allow_all = TRUE
)

observed

The second operation inspects retrieved observations, so the result is conditional on the request. It is not an implementation of SDMX ContentConstraint queries. Moreover, the example deliberately permits a potentially broad download and should be used with attention to response size.

For statistical work, this separation helps prevent a common misunderstanding: the universe of valid categories is not necessarily the same as the categories populated by the data.

5 Documentation and Current Scope

The package includes documentation on authentication, Dataflow discovery, DSD metadata, filtering, observed availability, and code-label decoding. Rather than repeating those guides here, I recommend starting with the Getting Started guide and the function reference.

The initial version is deliberately focused. tuiksdmx is an SDMX client, not a general-purpose interface to every resource on the TÜİK portal. It does not claim to support every SDMX service feature or every Dataflow without further testing. Provider structures and authentication behaviour can change, so reproducible work still requires validation and sensible request boundaries.

6 Final Thoughts

When working with an API, it is tempting to judge a client only by how quickly it returns a table. For structured statistical data, I think a more useful measure is whether we can identify what we requested, validate the choices we made, and reproduce the result later.

That is the idea behind tuiksdmx: bring discovery, statistical metadata, validation, and data retrieval into the same R workflow while keeping the raw SDMX machinery largely out of the way.

I welcome feedback, reproducible bug reports, and contributions through the project repository. The package is an independently developed open-source project, not an official TÜİK software product.

Project links: GitHub repository · Package website · Guides · Issues and suggestions

7 References

  • SDMX. Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange. https://sdmx.org/.
  • Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK). Official website. https://www.tuik.gov.tr/.
  • Tüzen, M. F. (2026). tuiksdmx: Access the Turkish Statistical Institute SDMX REST API (version 0.1.0). GitHub. https://github.com/MFatihTuzen/tuiksdmx.
  • Tüzen, M. F. tuiksdmx package documentation. https://mfatihtuzen.github.io/tuiksdmx/.
